metadata.proof: SOURCE: customer contact adds a comment on an escalation in WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER status → SINK: escalation.status is directly set to OPEN and saved via escalation.save(), bypassing escalation.transition_to() which would validate the transition against ESCALATION_TRANSITIONS dict (models.py lines 244-255). While WAITING_ON_CUSTOMER→OPEN is currently valid, any future change to the transition rules will not be enforced here because the code bypasses the validation method entirely.

extra.message: Account takeover: platform admin can change any user's email/username enabling password-reset hijack

metadata.proof: SOURCE: UserAdminForm.email field (forms.py line 229) accepts arbitrary email via POST from platform admin → SINK: save() at lines 284-285 sets both user.email and user.username (the login credential) to the form value. A malicious platform admin changes a target user's email to attacker@evil.com, then initiates password reset for that email — the reset link goes to the attacker. The only protections are against self-disable (line 266) and self-demotion (lines 275-278) — there is no protection against modifying other users and no second-factor or confirmation required.

extra.message: File upload validated by extension and size only — no content inspection for malicious payloads

metadata.proof: SOURCE: request.FILES['file'] → validation chain: (1) DocumentForm.clean_file (forms.py lines 199-202) only checks size <= 5MB; (2) FileExtensionValidator on model (models.py line 370) only checks extension against ['pdf','csv','txt','docx','xlsx']. No magic-byte inspection, no antivirus scan, no content-type verification. An attacker renames malware.exe to invoice.pdf and uploads — the file is stored and served with the original filename. Combined with the Content-Type preserved from upload (views.py line 689), the file is served with whatever metadata the attacker provided.

extra.message: Password reset does not invalidate existing API keys or webhook secrets

metadata.proof: Django's PasswordResetConfirmView changes the user's password but does not revoke API keys or rotate webhook secrets created by that user. If an attacker compromises a user's credentials (or an API key secret), the victim resetting their password does not invalidate the stolen API key (APIKey.status remains ACTIVE). API keys are organization-scoped but created_by tracks the user. No hook exists to cascade revocation on password change.

extra.message: Missing authenticated password-change endpoint — users cannot change their own password

metadata.proof: The urlpatterns contain login, logout, and password-reset (forgotten password) routes, but no password_change or password_change_done routes. Authenticated users who know their password have no endpoint to change it. The only path to a new password is the public password-reset flow, which relies on email delivery and a reset token — an unnecessary friction that discourages regular password rotation.
